On February 3, 2024, MCM Design [Michael Matte] posted his Report 6, Part 2, called "Piggy-Backing 2 Composite Video Driver Schemes onto an Astec RF Modulator."

It has taken me two months to finally reply to Michael's post, but I knew that I would get to it eventually.  I enjoyed reading his fact-filled article/report.  Also, the provided pictures were helpful to follow along with the article. The document in the post is quite technical and full of facts, such as part numbers and the pins numbers used to solder for the SMD chip. This makes the reading quite "heavy," which likely limits the number of readers. It will be a great addition to BallyAlley, once it makes its way there.  As a reference document, Michael's posts are a treasure.

Michael asked, "[Would] lowering the series R33 resistor to 1K ohms [...] increase the custom data chip's video output line [...] which might raise the chip's operating temperature[?]"

Is there anyone here with hardware experience who can duplicate Michael's composite modifications and then test the results with a temperature meter or infrared temperature gun?

Michael continued, "Users who run their Astrocade with the console top in place should probably not attempt any R33 modification."

I never have my Astrocade's top portion of the console when I'm using it. I don't have the RF shielding in place in either.  There have been conflicting reports throughout the years on the Astrocade discussion group whether this makes any difference. For me, not using the top is a must to prevent overheating. Others have said that they have accidentally "zapped" an IC chip when removing the RF shielding, which for them has had devastating results.

Michael said, "I ran some low-res games [with this composite mod]. My reaction was wow! [...] What a major improvement compared to the RF modulated display."

I wish I could have the same experience: a clean, clear picture on a TV. I've never used a composite mod on my own Astrocade. I have used the s-video upgrade, but I get ghosting and the colors that are displayed are also affected. I would prefer composite-out as it is more useful in a variety of situations. For example, my video capture card uses composite input directly.
 
Michael finishes his post with, "Welcome to the world of composite video. Say goodbye to modulated video."

I am so used to using RF-out from my Astrocade that I wouldn't know what to do if the TV interference disappeared.  It might be like losing an old friend, but maybe a friend who has grown a bit annoying over the years.

Thanks for taking the time to write about these different composite upgrade options for the Bally Arcade/Astrocade, Michael.

As a result of spending time the last several days examining Perkins hi-res motherboard scheme, MCM Design has been inspired and has come up with a cleaner variation of Perkins hi-res vision.

Here are a few details.

THE SCREEN RAM BOARD

This board would be 2 1/2 x 3 inches and rest on top of the Astrocade motherboard DRAM area.

The board would include:
4 Static RAM (SRAM) - DS
4 74LS245 - DS
4 74LS166 - DS
1 74F373 in a socket

DS = Double Stacked
The bottom chip in each stack would be in a socket.
The top chip would be cleanly stacked and fairly easy to replace if it failed.

CONTROL LINES BOARD

This board would rest on top of the motherboard between the custom Address, I/O chips and the Z80.

The board would include MCMs software low/hi-res mode select scheme.

COMPOSITE VIDEO OUTPUT

The RF modulator would be piggybacked with MCMs composite video driver scheme plus an audio coupler line.

A 3.5mm dual line output jack would allow connection to a TV/Monitor.

MISCELLANEOUS INFO

Some #30 wrapping wires would be fed through a few existing motherboard holes and soldered to motherboard bottom solder pads.

Some #30 wrapping wires would lie on top of the motherboard.

Both the low or hi-res graphic modes would be full screen displays.

Normal power on would be in the low-res mode.

The hi-res mode could be accessed (displayed) via the cartridge connector or the 50 pin expansion.

NOTES:

All 8 DRAM and the U23 DM81LS95 chips would have to be desoldered.

A remote +5v power supply would be required for the 2 add-on boards.

The console top would not be usable.

There would be no medium-res mode.

Perhaps Gambits could upgrade the Lil' White RAM to include hi-res compatibility.

This is not an April fools joke.

FINAL COMMENTS

When would MCM Design build a prototype motherboard?
That is a very good question.
Who other than MCM would be interested in modifying their Astrocade? Anyone?

MCM Design

Why does MCM Design utilize 4 screen static RAM chips for the hi-res mode?

Why not use just one 16KB (or larger) static RAM chip and decode it into four 4KB banks, instead of using four 4KB (or larger) SRAM chips?

Unfortunately in the hi-res mode, the custom address/data chips scan (read) for the TV display, 1 byte of data from each of the required 4 screen RAM banks SIMULTANEOUSLY.

That's why four 74LS166 8 bit shift register chips are normally used for the hi-res mode. The simultaneous four bytes (32 bits) are shifted into the two custom data chip Serial 0 and Serial 1 inputs using a 7Mhz clock, during every TV display scan attempt.

If someone can create a hi-res screen RAM scheme using just 1 SRAM chip and also meet the 4 simultaneous byte read requirement for all 4 screen RAM banks during the TV display scan, MCM Design would like to see that created scheme.

"Arcade Alley" [1st Arcade Awards].
by Bill Kunkel and Frank T. Laney II.
VIDEO magazine (March 1980).

[The Bally-related material from this article has been transcribed here.]

Best Audio & Visual Effects
Bally

It beeps, it bangs, it jingles, it chimes-- and the games explode off the screen in a rainbow of colors. Nothing creates that delightful arcade atmosphere like superior sound and visual effects, and the Bally system is the undisputed champ in this regard.

Decades of dominance in the pinball machine business have made Bally conscious of the fact that a truly complete game must sound and look right in addition to playing well. Their games are a symphony of fluid animation, vibrant color, and tasteful sound effects. It's "window dressing" like this that elevates game like Bally Football to the level of home arcade masterpiece.

Best Sports Game
Football (Bally)

This game provides arcade lovers with an amazing amount of pigskin action-- including inside and outside running, pass interceptions, quarterback sacks, razzle-dazzle plays, and even a "mad dog" linebacker on defense! Would-be quarterbacks can select from a wide range of plays, with the available choices altering to reflect current field position.

The best part is that Bally wisely decided not to squeeze the whole gridiron on the screen at the same time. Instead of squinting at a tiny full-size field, players luxuriate in the detailed presentation of the 40-yard segment that is actually the focus of the action. When a play goes for an unusually long gain, the next 40-yard section automatically fills the screen.

Best Commercial Arcade Game
Space Invaders (Bally)

The most popular new arcade attraction since electronic games began, Space Invaders first caught on in Japan; schoolchildren in the country cut classes en mass in order to feed their yen to this ingenious machine. Bally purchased the U.S. rights, reworked the design into a more conventional upright format, and immediately found that Americans love it too.

Players maneuver a laser cannon horizontally along the bottom of the playfield while five columns of space monsters march down the screen, firing the weapons as they come. Players have the extra advantage of four protective bunkers, but these are gradually disintegrated by incoming and outgoing fire. The game gives three rounds of play for 25 cents, a round ending whenever the invaders successfully blast player's cannon.

names/licenses/etc. being on those two rather than the Astrocade (which

Even the Odyssey2 was going to beat it on distribution, which was, to my
mind, the biggest factor working against the Astrocade's potential for
wider success (the software (which was another big issue) *may* have sorted
itself out with wider distribution leading to great sales, etc.).

The columns in Video were indeed the original OG of mass market video game
journalism, leading directly to the legendary Electronic Games (with "Frank
Laney" really being Arnie Katz, of course -
http://www.gooddealgames.com/articles/Electronic%20Games%20Magazine%20First%20Cover.html
(and let's not forget the concurrent newsletter-style publication they
produced for a time)). If you read the early issues of Electronic Games,
they still had a fondness for the Astrocade, but it became increasingly
clear where the true focus was going to remain, if for nothing more than
practical business reasons. Even as a kid in New Jersey, when I went to
various retailers I only recall, on the console side, Atari 2600,
Intellivision, and Odyssey2 early on, and don't think I ever did see an
Astrocade. It was only in the pages of Electronic Games that I was exposed
to it then.

I say all of that because I'd like you guys to allow me a few words about Bill, since this column and the "Arkies" have been mentioned. It's as good an opportunity as any to remember the strong character of the Game Doctor.

Ed Averett's O2 game K.C. Munchkin! was released by North-American Philips / Magnavox in November of 1981. It was un-released by Atari, so to speak, in March of '82. The latter company claimed in court that the game was unacceptably similar to Pac-Man, whose home versions it held the rights to.

Whereas N.A.P. had initially prevailed, Atari won the case on appeal. It was probably this verdict that scared Astrocade out of releasing Muncher. Just my conjecture, though.

Bill Kunkel risked the perks of his career as a game journalist by testifying against Atari. He rightly felt that K.C. Munchkin! contained enough differences to be considered a unique game. This display of integrity was, and obviously remains, uncharacteristic of most people in the "journalistic" profession. Considering that Atari was the giant at the time, it's really something that Bill held neither livelihood nor corporate favoritism above principle. We could use a few more like him.

Thanks for indulging me. Anyway, great scans!

"Arcade Alley" [1st Arcade Awards].
by Bill Kunkel and Frank T. Laney II.
VIDEO magazine (March 1980).

[The Bally-related material from this article has been transcribed here.]

Best Audio & Visual Effects
Bally

It beeps, it bangs, it jingles, it chimes-- and the games explode off the screen in a rainbow of colors. Nothing creates that delightful arcade atmosphere like superior sound and visual effects, and the Bally system is the undisputed champ in this regard.

Decades of dominance in the pinball machine business have made Bally conscious of the fact that a truly complete game must sound and look right in addition to playing well. Their games are a symphony of fluid animation, vibrant color, and tasteful sound effects. It's "window dressing" like this that elevates game like Bally Football to the level of home arcade masterpiece.

Best Sports Game
Football (Bally)

This game provides arcade lovers with an amazing amount of pigskin action-- including inside and outside running, pass interceptions, quarterback sacks, razzle-dazzle plays, and even a "mad dog" linebacker on defense! Would-be quarterbacks can select from a wide range of plays, with the available choices altering to reflect current field position.

The best part is that Bally wisely decided not to squeeze the whole gridiron on the screen at the same time. Instead of squinting at a tiny full-size field, players luxuriate in the detailed presentation of the 40-yard segment that is actually the focus of the action. When a play goes for an unusually long gain, the next 40-yard section automatically fills the screen.

Best Commercial Arcade Game
Space Invaders (Bally)

The most popular new arcade attraction since electronic games began, Space Invaders first caught on in Japan; schoolchildren in the country cut classes en mass in order to feed their yen to this ingenious machine. Bally purchased the U.S. rights, reworked the design into a more conventional upright format, and immediately found that Americans love it too.

Players maneuver a laser cannon horizontally along the bottom of the playfield while five columns of space monsters march down the screen, firing the weapons as they come. Players have the extra advantage of four protective bunkers, but these are gradually disintegrated by incoming and outgoing fire. The game gives three rounds of play for 25 cents, a round ending whenever the invaders successfully blast player's cannon.

On April 22, 2024, Ken Lill wrote, "When John released the 4K Blue Ram kit, it came with a form of Blue Ram Basic on tape. It might have been Blue Ram Basic 1.0. If we can find a 4K BR, maybe the owner will have a copy of the tape?!?!"

I believe that Ken is referring to "Blue Ram OS 1.0" by Perkins Engineering.  It was written for Bally BASIC with 4K (or more?) of RAM and the Blue Ram Expansion Unit.  This 300-baud version of this BASIC is archived on BallyAlley.com.  On BallyAlley, this information is written about the program:

'Most users of the Blue Ram expansion unit are aware of "Blue Ram BASIC 1.1," as eventually it became Perkin Engineering's standard method to program any extended RAM beyond the original 4K that shipped with the Bally Arcade/Astrocade console. The program that first shipped on 300-baud tape allowed BASIC users to access extended memory, "Blue Ram OS 1.0," is a hybrid between Bally BASIC and newly written routines which allow access to extended RAM.

'"Blue Ram OS 1.0" is not similar AT ALL to "Blue Ram BASIC 1.1." If you read through the "Blue Ram OS 1.0" documentation then you'll see that you would have had access to 1.8K of RAM (the screen RAM normally available to BASIC), plus another 3.8K of RAM available on the Blue Ram unit (meaning this was meant for the first Blue Ram expansions shipped). It seems that using "Blue Ram OS 1.0" would have popped you in and out of Bally BASIC and the Blue Ram OS depending on what you were doing. This operating system definitely seems like a stop-gap measure so that people that bought the Blue Ram expansion would have SOME way to use it besides only programming it in machine language. Giving BASIC users access to extended RAM was a great idea. This program was eventually followed up with "Blue Ram BASIC 1.1," which was a full-fledged BASIC that didn't require "Bally BASIC" at all.'

The brief, 5-page instructions for this preliminary operating system for the original 4K Blue Ram expansion unit are here:

https://www.ballyalley.com/perkins/perkins_blue_ram_os_1.0.pdf

The "Blue Ram OS 1.0" can be downloaded in 300-BAUD format here:

https://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/ram_expansion_required/perkins_engineering/Blue%20RAM%20OS%201.0%20(1981)(Perkins%20Engineering).zip

Does anyone have experience with this way of taking advantage of the additional RAM of the Blue Ram unit using "Bally BASIC?"

The Blue Ram Keyboard from Perkins engineering originally was wire-wrapped. They later designed a PC Board for it. There were a couple of problems with the board, so they had to put jumper(s) and had to cut at least 1 trace. If yours is like that you have the best one they made. I still have a couple of bare boards and maybe even a diagram of how it was modified. It probably take me a month of Sundays to find them in my garage storage. If you plug the keyboard into the furthest set of ping in the BRB socket, the keyboard should work. Did you get the wall adapter for the BRB unit? It is a 9V, center positive 2.5mm plug. If you need any help getting the unit going, please drop me a line. I'll be glad to help.
Ken Lill   kenzre@yahoo.com or through the group here.
P.S. I can't wait to here that you have the Blue Ram up and running.
P.P.S. The Keyboard is normally operated in the caps lock on position. This gives all caps to the alphabet characters. The caps lock off will give you the "words" position. You even have the new words as tokens, like Snap, Show, point, Zero, etc.

21400: After further investigation, I guess we are both right regarding the value of CX.  I get -71 because my program prints out the value in memory location 4E5C (VDMX), which would be the second leftmost character position due to the leftmost character position being taken up by the > prompt.  You get -77 because when you issue a PRINT CX statement in direct mode, the cursor position moves to the leftmost character position, which is -77, and that is what is printed out.  PRINT CX in direct mode will always print -77 in AstroBasic.  In other words, the value of CX is pretty darned irrelevant.

https://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml.html

The ZMac assembler and the header file are here:

https://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_tools/ml_tools.html

In 2016, I wrote an article on how to set-up Zmac.  It is here:

https://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/ml_docs.html#ProgrammingTheBallyArcade-Astrocade

The information in the article is a bit outdated and will likely use tools that may not be what you require exactly, but the article should get you up-and-running if you're familiar with Z80 assembly language already.

Let us know if you need more help.
